cards.front: Adding interferon to human cells switches on target genes within minutes even when a drug blocks all new protein synthesis. What does this result establish?
cards.back: Every protein that carries the signal from interferon to the target genes is already present in the cell before interferon arrives.
cards.why: Because translation is blocked, the pathway cannot rely on synthesizing an intermediate factor and must activate pre-existing proteins.
cards.quote: a specific set of genes switches on within minutes—even when a drug has blocked all new protein synthesis.

cards.front: Why did investigators studying interferon signaling judge classical second messengers to be a poor fit for relaying the signal to target genes?
cards.back: A rise in a second messenger is fairly nonspecific, whereas interferon produces a highly specific transcriptional response.
cards.quote: a rise in a second messenger is fairly nonspecific, whereas interferon's transcriptional response is highly specific.
cards.section: Finding the two parts in 1992

cards.front: Interferon drives tyrosine phosphorylation on proteins of the DNA-binding complex ISGF3, and the broad kinase inhibitor staurosporine blocks ISGF3 activation. What did this experiment show?
cards.back: It placed a tyrosine kinase upstream of the DNA-binding complex ISGF3 without naming which kinase was responsible.
cards.quote: That placed a tyrosine kinase upstream of the DNA-binding factor without naming which one.
cards.section: Finding the two parts in 1992

cards.front: Human cells are engineered so an interferon-responsive DNA element controls a marker gene that kills expressing cells in selective medium. When interferon is added after mutagenesis, which cells survive and why?
cards.back: Only interferon-deaf mutant cells survive. Cells with an intact pathway respond to interferon, switch on the lethal marker gene, and die.
cards.quote: in the chosen medium, any cell that still answered interferon switched on the marker and died, leaving only interferon-deaf mutants alive.
cards.section: Finding the two parts in 1992

cards.front: Putting normal genomic DNA into a mutant cell line to identify a broken gene by restoring the lost response is called {{c1::complementation}}.
cards.back: The DNA taken up by the rescued cell carries a working copy of the broken gene.
cards.quote: The DNA that cell took up carries a working copy of the broken gene. This test is called complementation.
cards.section: Finding the two parts in 1992

cards.front: Four recessive interferon-deaf human mutant lines (A, B, C, D) are fused pairwise. Hybrids A+B and C+D fail to respond to interferon, whereas A+C, A+D, B+C, and B+D all respond. What is the smallest number of pathway genes mutated across the four lines, and why?
cards.back: Two genes: one mutated in both A and B, and another mutated in both C and D. Recessive mutants rescue each other only when each parent supplies a working copy of the gene broken in the other.
cards.quote: Put normal genomic DNA into the mutant cells and look for the rare cell whose interferon response returns.
cards.section: Finding the two parts in 1992

cards.front: In Pellegrini's 1992 DNA rescue of an interferon-deaf human mutant line, the rescuing gene encoded the tyrosine kinase {{c1::TYK2}}.
cards.back: TYK2 is one of the four mammalian JAKs.
cards.quote: her group reported the rescuing gene for one mutant: it encoded the tyrosine kinase TYK2.
cards.section: Finding the two parts in 1992

cards.front: STAT stands for {{c1::signal transducers and activators of transcription}}.
cards.back: DNA-binding proteins that carry phosphotyrosine after cytokine stimulation.
cards.quote: Darnell's laboratory named those proteins STATs (signal transducers and activators of transcription).
cards.section: Finding the two parts in 1992

cards.front: Name four hormones that signal through the same class I and class II cytokine receptor family used by interferons and interleukins?
cards.back: Erythropoietin (EPO), growth hormone, prolactin, and leptin.
cards.quote: erythropoietin (EPO), which tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells, along with growth hormone, prolactin, and leptin.
cards.section: Inside the relay: activation loops, two grips, and built-in restraint

cards.front: How does a class I or class II cytokine receptor differ from a receptor tyrosine kinase like the insulin receptor, and where does its kinase activity come from?
cards.back: It crosses the membrane once with no catalytic domain of its own; instead, a stretch of its inner tail near the membrane holds a separate JAK tyrosine kinase before cytokine arrives.
cards.quote: a class I or class II cytokine receptor crosses the membrane once and has no catalytic domain of its own.
cards.section: Inside the relay: activation loops, two grips, and built-in restraint

cards.front: Mammals have four Janus kinases: {{c1::JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, and TYK2}}.
cards.quote: Mammals have four JAKs: JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, and TYK2.
cards.section: Inside the relay: activation loops, two grips, and built-in restraint

cards.front: What are the two kinase-like domains side by side in each JAK, and what is the role of the non-catalytic domain at rest?
cards.back: A working kinase domain and a pseudokinase domain, which has the kinase fold with little or no catalytic activity and restrains the working kinase at rest.
cards.quote: a working kinase and a pseudokinase domain, which has the kinase fold but little or no catalytic activity and restrains the working kinase at rest.
cards.section: Inside the relay: activation loops, two grips, and built-in restraint

cards.front: When cytokine binding positions two receptor-bound JAKs against each other, they turn both kinases fully on by phosphorylating each other's {{c1::activation loops}}.
cards.back: This mutual step is trans-phosphorylation.
cards.quote: either way, the two JAKs phosphorylate each other's activation loops, the switch from the phosphorylation lesson, turning both kinases fully on.
cards.section: Inside the relay: activation loops, two grips, and built-in restraint

cards.front: How does a STAT protein's single SH2 domain act twice during JAK–STAT signaling?
cards.back: First it docks the latent STAT onto a phosphotyrosine on the receptor tail for phosphorylation by JAK; then it holds a partner STAT's phosphotyrosine in an active reciprocal dimer.
cards.quote: two phosphorylated STATs lock into a reciprocal dimer—each SH2 domain holding its partner's phosphotyrosine, two grips where one held the STAT to the receptor.
cards.section: Inside the relay: activation loops, two grips, and built-in restraint

cards.front: Every docking tyrosine on a cytokine receptor's inner tail is changed to phenylalanine, while the JAK-binding stretch, JAKs, and STATs remain normal. When cytokine binds, what happens to JAK activation and STAT phosphorylation, and why?
cards.back: JAKs still activate each other, but STAT phosphorylation fails. Receptor pairing still lets intact JAKs trans-phosphorylate each other's activation loops, yet without tail phosphotyrosines, STATs lose their SH2 docking sites beside the JAKs.
cards.quote: Without phosphotyrosines on the receptor tail, however, STATs lose their SH2 docking sites beside the JAKs, so STAT recruitment and phosphorylation fail.
cards.section: Inside the relay: activation loops, two grips, and built-in restraint

cards.front: A mutant STAT has its single C-terminal JAK phosphorylation site changed from tyrosine to phenylalanine, while the receptor, JAKs, and the STAT's SH2 domain are normal. When cytokine binds, what happens and why?
cards.back: JAK activation, receptor-tail phosphorylation, and STAT docking succeed, but reciprocal STAT dimerization fails. Because the mutated residue cannot be phosphorylated, no STAT phosphotyrosine exists for a partner's SH2 domain to grip.
cards.quote: the JAK phosphorylates a single tyrosine near the STAT's C-terminal end (tyrosine 701 in STAT1).
cards.section: Inside the relay: activation loops, two grips, and built-in restraint

cards.front: A cytokine activates both STAT1 and STAT3. In a DNA-binding assay, bound STAT dimers consist of 36% STAT3:STAT3 homodimers, 48% STAT1:STAT3 heterodimers, and 16% STAT1:STAT1 homodimers. What percentage of the individual STAT molecules in these bound dimers is STAT3?
cards.back: 60%. In 100 dimers (200 STAT molecules), STAT3 accounts for (36 × 2) + (48 × 1) = 120 molecules; 120 / 200 = 0.60, or 60% (equivalently, 36% + 48%/2 = 60%).
cards.quote: The active pair accumulates in the nucleus, binds a specific DNA sequence, and turns on transcription.
cards.section: Inside the relay: activation loops, two grips, and built-in restraint

cards.front: In a STAT protein, which domain grips a specific DNA sequence, and which region recruits the transcription machinery?
cards.back: The central DNA-binding domain grips the specific DNA sequence, and the C-terminal end recruits the transcription machinery.
cards.quote: the central DNA-binding domain grips DNA; and the C-terminal end recruits the transcription machinery.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What does the direct JAK–STAT relay gain, and what two capabilities does it give up compared with a three-kinase cascade?
cards.back: It gains speed and a direct line from occupied receptors to genes, while giving up multi-stage signal amplification and intermediate control points such as switches or pathway junctions.
cards.why: JAK is the only kinase, so no downstream kinase tier multiplies the signal again, and there are no intermediate tiers where other pathways can cut in.
cards.quote: What does this direct route give up? Multi-stage gain and intermediate control points.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A synthetic STAT keeps its SH2 domain, C-terminal phosphorylation-site tyrosine, and central DNA-binding domain, but loses the C-terminal region that recruits transcription machinery. When cytokine binds, predict what happens to dimerization, DNA binding, and transcription.
cards.back: Active STAT pairs still form, accumulate in the nucleus, and bind target DNA, but transcription fails to turn on. This rests on the rule that a STAT divides its five relay jobs among separate modules: SH2 and the C-terminal tyrosine drive docking and pairing, the central domain grips DNA, and the C-terminal end recruits transcription machinery.
cards.quote: A STAT has a module for each job: the SH2 domain detects phosphotyrosines on the active receptor; the single C-terminal tyrosine takes the phosphate
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How do dozens of distinct cytokines produce specific cellular responses while signaling through only four JAKs and seven STATs?
cards.back: Different cytokine receptor tails select specific JAKs and STATs, coupling each cytokine receptor to a distinct JAK–STAT combination.
cards.quote: Because receptor tails select specific JAKs and STATs, deleting one gene in knockout mice—or finding a natural mutation in a patient—shows which cytokines depend on it.
cards.section: Four JAKs, seven STATs: what knockouts and patients show

cards.front: In knockout mice, losing STAT1 eliminates responses to which cytokines, and what phenotype results?
cards.back: Interferons; STAT1-deficient mice have no interferon response and succumb to infections that normal mice survive.
cards.quote: No interferon response; mice succumb to infections normal mice survive
cards.section: Four JAKs, seven STATs: what knockouts and patients show

cards.front: A researcher deletes STAT3 throughout mouse embryos to study adult cytokine signaling, but recovers no adult knockout mice. Why does this happen, and how have STAT3's functions been mapped instead?
cards.back: STAT3 serves multiple developmental and cytokine signals so whole-embryo knockouts die early; therefore, its functions are mapped one tissue at a time.
cards.quote: Embryo dies early; functions mapped one tissue at a time
cards.section: Four JAKs, seven STATs: what knockouts and patients show

cards.front: Prolactin and growth-hormone signaling depend on {{c1::STAT5A and STAT5B}}, which partly cover for each other in knockout mice.
cards.quote: Failed prolactin and growth-hormone responses; the two partly cover for each other
cards.section: Four JAKs, seven STATs: what knockouts and patients show

cards.front: Mouse embryos lacking JAK2 are anaemic, die at about day 12.5 of gestation, and have no culturable red-cell precursors in fetal liver despite intact JAK1, JAK3, and TYK2. What does this show?
cards.back: The other three JAKs do not cover for JAK2 on the EPO receptor; adult-type red-cell production specifically requires JAK2.
cards.quote: held no red-cell precursors that could be grown in culture—even though the genes for JAK1, JAK3, and TYK2 are untouched.
cards.section: Four JAKs, seven STATs: what knockouts and patients show

cards.front: Boys with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) have mutations in the gamma chain of the interleukin-2 receptor, yet their immune defect is far more severe than losing interleukin-2 alone. What does this imply?
cards.back: Multiple cytokine receptors must share that subunit (the common gamma chain, used by receptors for IL-2, 4, 7, 9, 15, and 21), so breaking it silences an entire cluster of immune signals.
cards.quote: Several cytokine receptors must share that chain—now called the common gamma chain (used by receptors for interleukins 2, 4, 7, 9, 15, and 21)
cards.section: Four JAKs, seven STATs: what knockouts and patients show

cards.front: A child has SCID without T cells or natural killer cells, and her cells fail to answer common-gamma-chain cytokines despite making a normal common gamma chain. Which gene one step downstream is mutated, and why?
cards.back: Both copies of JAK3. Because JAK3 sits on the common gamma chain's tail, losing JAK3 silences the same set of interleukin receptors and produces the same SCID phenotype.
cards.quote: found a mutation in each copy of JAK3, the kinase on the gamma chain's tail
cards.section: Four JAKs, seven STATs: what knockouts and patients show

cards.front: How do tyrosine phosphatases switch off JAK–STAT signaling and reset STAT proteins?
cards.back: They strip phosphates from JAKs, receptor tails, and STATs; a STAT dephosphorylated in the nucleus returns to the cytoplasm ready for reuse.
cards.quote: Tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphates from JAKs, receptor tails, and STATs. A STAT dephosphorylated in the nucleus returns to the cytoplasm ready for reuse.
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: Delayed negative-feedback inhibitors encoded by STAT target genes are called {{c1::SOCS proteins}}.
cards.back: Suppressors of cytokine signaling.
cards.quote: SOCS proteins (suppressors of cytokine signaling) are themselves encoded by STAT target genes—delayed negative feedback, as in the signaling circuits lesson.
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: After using an SH2 domain to bind phosphotyrosines on active receptors and JAKs, by what two mechanisms can SOCS1 and SOCS3 shut down signaling?
cards.back: They directly block the JAK's substrate-binding groove, and they recruit a ubiquitin ligase that can mark the receptor complex for the proteasome.
cards.quote: Some, including SOCS1 and SOCS3, block the JAK's substrate-binding groove directly, and all carry a region that recruits a ubiquitin ligase
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: A cell can no longer induce SOCS proteins after cytokine stimulation, while its tyrosine phosphatases remain intact. How will its active STAT response differ from normal during and after cytokine exposure?
cards.back: Active STAT climbs higher and stays elevated longer while cytokine is present, because delayed negative feedback on the receptor–JAK complex is gone. Once cytokine stops, phosphatases still dephosphorylate STATs and reset the pathway.
cards.quote: Active STAT would climb higher and stay elevated longer while cytokine is present, because the delayed negative-feedback brake on the receptor–JAK complex is gone.
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: Cells are exposed to sustained cytokine stimulation in the presence of a protein synthesis inhibitor, while tyrosine phosphatases remain intact. Predict both the initial activation of STAT target genes and the subsequent attenuation of active STAT levels, and why.
cards.back: Target gene transcription still switches on within minutes, but SOCS delayed negative feedback fails, so active STAT climbs higher and stays elevated longer while cytokine is present. This rests on two stated rules: core JAK–STAT relay proteins already exist before cytokine arrives, whereas SOCS proteins must be newly produced from STAT target genes.
cards.quote: Suppose a cell can no longer induce SOCS proteins after cytokine stimulation, while its tyrosine phosphatases remain intact.
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: Most patients with polycythaemia vera carry the {{c1::V617F}} mutation in the pseudokinase domain of JAK2.
cards.back: Valine 617 changed to phenylalanine weakens pseudokinase restraint.
cards.quote: valine 617 of JAK2 changed to phenylalanine (V617F). Residue 617 sits in the pseudokinase domain.
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: A patient has too many red blood cells and low blood erythropoietin (EPO). Bone-marrow progenitors form red-cell colonies in culture without EPO (healthy cells form none), and a JAK2 inhibitor abolishes those colonies. What explains all three observations?
cards.back: A mutant JAK2 (with weakened pseudokinase restraint) is constitutively active without EPO, driving excess red-cell production even when circulating EPO is low.
cards.quote: helps two JAK2 molecules hold together in the active pair, so JAK2 signals from the EPO receptor with little or no EPO present.
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: Why is anaemia a known side effect of ATP-pocket JAK inhibitors used for autoimmune disease, and how does targeting a JAK's pseudokinase domain instead improve selectivity?
cards.back: Anaemia occurs because the ATP pockets of the four JAKs are very similar, so ATP-pocket drugs partly inhibit JAK2 and blunt EPO-driven red-cell production. A drug that binds one JAK's pseudokinase domain and locks it in its restraining state can block that JAK while sparing the others.
cards.quote: The ATP pockets of the four JAKs are very similar, so drugs aimed there struggle to distinguish one JAK from another and partly inhibit JAK2—blunting EPO-driven red-cell production.
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: Why did JAK3 SCID inspire tofacitinib for rheumatoid arthritis, and how does tofacitinib's actual selectivity differ from that rationale?
cards.back: Patients lacking JAK3 have an immune defect with little else, suggesting tissue selectivity; however, tofacitinib competes at the ATP pocket and inhibits JAK1 as strongly as JAK3, plus JAK2 weakly.
cards.quote: In practice, tofacitinib inhibits JAK1 as strongly as JAK3—and JAK2 more weakly—with much of its clinical effect coming through JAK1.
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: The psoriasis drug {{c1::deucravacitinib}} binds the pseudokinase domain of TYK2 and locks it in its restraining state, sparing JAK1, JAK2, and JAK3.
cards.quote: deucravacitinib, approved for psoriasis, binds the pseudokinase domain of TYK2 and holds it in its restraining state, blocking TYK2 while sparing JAK1, JAK2, and JAK3.
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: Compare treating JAK2 V617F polycythaemia vera with ruxolitinib (an ATP-pocket JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor) versus deucravacitinib. Predict which drug suppresses the excess red-cell production and why.
cards.back: Only ruxolitinib suppresses the excess red-cell production; deucravacitinib would not be expected to. This rests on two stated rules: JAK2 V617F drives red-cell overproduction by signaling from the EPO receptor without EPO, whereas deucravacitinib locks TYK2's pseudokinase domain in its restraining state while sparing JAK1, JAK2, and JAK3.
cards.quote: Ruxolitinib, which inhibits JAK1 and JAK2, was approved in the United States in 2011 for myelofibrosis, a bone-marrow disease related to polycythaemia vera.
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: Suppose a cell expresses both constitutively active JAK2 V617F and an EPO receptor whose tail docking tyrosines have all been changed to phenylalanine. Without EPO added, predict whether STATs are phosphorylated and why.
cards.back: STAT phosphorylation still fails. This rests on two stated rules: although V617F weakens pseudokinase restraint so JAK2 signals without EPO, STAT recruitment and phosphorylation still require phosphotyrosine docking sites on the receptor tail for the STAT's SH2 domain.
cards.quote: The change weakens that domain's restraint and helps two JAK2 molecules hold together in the active pair
cards.section: Turning signaling off, stuck-on JAK2, and targeted drugs

cards.front: How do crystal structures and live-cell single-molecule tracking disagree on when cytokine receptor chains such as the EPO receptor pair, and what conclusion holds either way?
cards.back: Crystal structures suggest chains are loosely pre-paired and hormone resets their angle, whereas single-molecule tracking points to ligand-induced pairing; either way, ligand binding positions two JAKs for trans-phosphorylation.
cards.quote: Single-molecule tracking of receptor chains in living cells points the other way, toward chains coming together when hormone binds.
cards.section: Do cytokine receptors pair before or after the cytokine binds?

cards.front: One growth hormone molecule has two different surfaces that each grip one copy of the same receptor chain. If cells are treated with a mutant growth hormone whose second binding surface is broken while the first remains normal, predict the effect on JAK activation and STAT signaling.
cards.back: JAK trans-phosphorylation and STAT signaling would be expected to fail. This rests on two stated rules: one growth hormone must grip two copies of the receptor chain using its two surfaces, and ligand binding must place two JAKs in position to trans-phosphorylate each other's activation loops.
cards.quote: One growth hormone molecule carries two different surfaces, each gripping one copy of the same receptor chain.
cards.section: Do cytokine receptors pair before or after the cytokine binds?

cards.front: A human cell carries two copies of nearly every gene. If a random mutagen independently disables a single copy of a pathway gene with probability 10^-4 per copy, how many cells out of 10^8 mutagenized cells are expected to have both copies of that specific gene disabled?
cards.back: 1 cell. Probability both copies are disabled independently = (10^-4)^2 = 10^-8 per cell; in 10^8 cells, expected double-knockout cells = 10^8 × 10^-8 = 1.
cards.why: Diploidy is why colleagues doubted Pellegrini's genetic screen could succeed.
cards.quote: A human cell carries two copies of nearly every gene, so many colleagues doubted a random mutagen could disable both copies of a pathway gene while keeping the cell alive.
cards.section: Inside Pellegrini's 1992 screen and the ISGF3 complex

cards.front: Which three proteins assemble to form the ISGF3 complex that binds interferon-responsive DNA during type I interferon signaling?
cards.back: STAT1, STAT2, and the partner protein IRF9.
cards.quote: Beyond simple STAT pairs, type I interferons assemble ISGF3—STAT1, STAT2, and the partner protein IRF9—to bind interferon-responsive DNA.
cards.section: Inside Pellegrini's 1992 screen and the ISGF3 complex

cards.front: What open question is posed by interleukin-6 and interleukin-10 signaling, and what explanation has been proposed?
cards.back: Both signal mainly through STAT3 yet produce largely opposite effects on inflammation; differences in how long the STAT3 signal lasts have been proposed, though the question is not settled.
cards.quote: interleukin-6 and interleukin-10 both signal mainly through STAT3, yet produce largely opposite effects on inflammation.
cards.section: One STAT, opposite outcomes

cards.front: Suppose a cell can no longer induce SOCS proteins. What would happen to the height and duration of the STAT3 signal after cytokine stimulation, and is it settled that this explains how IL-6 and IL-10 differ?
cards.back: Active STAT, STAT3 included, would climb higher and stay elevated longer, because SOCS proteins are delayed negative feedback that limits active STAT during cytokine exposure. Whether differences in STAT3 signal duration explain IL-6 versus IL-10 outcomes has only been proposed and is not settled.
cards.quote: Differences in how long the STAT3 signal lasts have been proposed, and the question is not settled.
cards.section: One STAT, opposite outcomes
